title: Is the blood in your veins blue?
hook: Anyone who has had blood drawn knows the answer.
summary: Never: blood is always red. Veins look blue because of the way skin scatters red light.

cardBlocks.text: Human blood is never blue. Oxygen-rich blood, mostly in the arteries, is bright red; blood that has given up its oxygen, mostly in the veins, is dark red. Anyone who has given blood or had a blood test can confirm it: venous blood comes out dark, but red. The veins themselves, by the way, are mostly colourless.

So why do they look blue? Because we see them through layers of skin and fat. According to a study by the physicist Alwin Kienle, skin scatters much of the red part of white light before it can reflect off the blood, leaving blue light to bounce back to our eyes. It’s a similar effect to the red sun at sunset.
Blood is always red; veins look blue because skin scatters red light before it can reach your eyes.

deepDiveBlocks.text: At sunset the atmosphere scatters blue colours away and the sun looks red. Skin does something similar, scattering the red light before it reflects off the blood.
A vein’s colour comes from the blood inside it, not from the vessel wall, which is mostly colourless.
